title: Chapter 89 — Fast-Fish and Loose-Fish
paragraphs: The mention of the marker-pole in the chapter before last calls for some account of the laws and regulations of the whale fishery, of which the marker may be considered the grand symbol and badge.

It frequently happens that when several ships are cruising together, a whale may be struck by one vessel, then escape, and finally be killed and captured by another. And within this general situation are many minor variations, all sharing this one feature. For example: after a weary and perilous chase and capture of a whale, the body may break loose from the ship in a violent storm and drift far to leeward, only to be retaken by a second whaler who, in a calm, snugly tows it alongside without risk of life or line. Thus the most maddening and violent disputes would constantly arise between fishermen, were there not some written or unwritten, universal, undisputed law applicable to all cases.

Perhaps the only formal whaling code authorized by legislation was that of Holland, decreed by the States-General in 1695. But though no other nation has ever had any written whaling law, the American fishermen have been their own legislators and lawyers in this matter. They have provided a system which for terse completeness surpasses Justinian's Pandects and the bylaws of the Chinese Society for the Suppression of Meddling with Other People's Business. Yes, these laws might be engraved on a Queen Anne's farthing, or the barb of a harpoon, and worn around the neck, so small are they.
I. A Fast-Fish belongs to the party fast to it.
II. A Loose-Fish is fair game for anybody who can soonest catch it.
But what causes trouble with this masterful code is the admirable brevity of it, which requires a vast volume of commentary to explain it.

First: What is a Fast-Fish? Alive or dead, a fish is technically fast when it is connected with an occupied ship or boat by any medium at all controllable by the occupant or occupants — a mast, an oar, a nine-inch cable, a telegraph wire, or a strand of cobweb, it is all the same. Likewise, a fish is technically fast when it bears a marker or any other recognized symbol of possession, so long as the marking party plainly shows both its ability to take the fish alongside at any time, and its intention to do so.

These are the learned commentaries. But the commentaries of the whalemen themselves sometimes consist of hard words and harder knocks — the fists doing the arguing. True, among the more upright and honorable whalemen, allowances are always made for special cases where it would be an outrageous moral injustice for one party to claim possession of a whale previously chased or killed by another. But others are by no means so scrupulous.

Some fifty years ago there was a curious case of whale-trover litigated in England. The plaintiffs stated that after a hard chase of a whale in the northern seas, and when they had succeeded in harpooning the fish, they were at last, through peril of their lives, obliged to abandon not only their lines but their boat itself. Eventually the defendants — the crew of another ship — came up with the whale, struck, killed, seized, and finally claimed it before the very eyes of the plaintiffs. And when those defendants were confronted, their captain snapped his fingers in the plaintiffs' faces and assured them that by way of celebration, he would now retain their line, harpoons, and boat, which had remained attached to the whale at the time of the seizure. Wherefore the plaintiffs sued for the recovery of the value of their whale, line, harpoons, and boat.

Mr. Erskine was counsel for the defendants; Lord Ellenborough was the judge. In the course of the defense, the witty Erskine went on to illustrate his position by alluding to a recent adultery case, in which a gentleman, after in vain trying to curb his wife's unfaithfulness, had at last abandoned her upon the seas of life. But in the course of years, repenting of that step, he brought an action to recover possession of her. Erskine was on the other side and had then supported the case by saying that though the gentleman had originally harpooned the lady, and had once had her fast, and only by reason of the great force of her wayward plunging had at last abandoned her — yet abandon her he did, so that she became a Loose-Fish. And therefore when a subsequent gentleman re-harpooned her, the lady then became that subsequent gentleman's property, along with whatever harpoon might have been found sticking in her.
Now in the present case Erskine argued that the examples of the whale and the lady were mutually illustrative of each other.

These arguments and counter-arguments being duly heard, the very learned judge officially decided as follows: As for the boat, he awarded it to the plaintiffs, because they had merely abandoned it to save their lives. But with regard to the disputed whale, harpoons, and line, they belonged to the defendants — the whale because it was a Loose-Fish at the time of the final capture, and the harpoons and line because when the fish made off with them, it acquired property in those articles, and hence anybody who afterward took the fish had a right to them. Now the defendants afterward took the fish; therefore, the aforesaid articles were theirs.

An ordinary man looking at this decision of the very learned judge might possibly object to it. But plowed down to the bedrock of the matter, the two great principles laid down in the twin whaling laws previously quoted — applied and explained by Lord Ellenborough in the above-cited case — these two laws touching Fast-Fish and Loose-Fish will, on reflection, be found the fundamentals of all human law. For notwithstanding its complicated decorative sculpture, the Temple of the Law, like the Temple of the Philistines, has but two pillars to stand on.

Is it not a saying on everyone's lips that possession is half the law — regardless of how the thing came into possession? But often possession is the whole of the law. What are the bodies and souls of Russian serfs and American slaves but Fast-Fish, of which possession is the whole of the law? What to the greedy landlord is the widow's last penny but a Fast-Fish? What is yonder undetected villain's marble mansion with a nameplate for a marker — what is that but a Fast-Fish? What is the ruinous discount that Mordecai the broker gets from poor Woebegone the bankrupt, on a loan to keep Woebegone's family from starving — what is that ruinous discount but a Fast-Fish? What is the Archbishop of Savesoul's income of a hundred thousand pounds, seized from the meager bread and cheese of hundreds of thousands of broken-backed laborers, all sure of heaven without any of Savesoul's help — what is that vast sum but a Fast-Fish? What are the Duke of Dunder's hereditary towns and hamlets but Fast-Fish? What to that mighty harpooner John Bull is poor Ireland but a Fast-Fish? What to that apostolic lancer Brother Jonathan is Texas but a Fast-Fish? And concerning all these, is not Possession the whole of the law?
But if the doctrine of Fast-Fish is pretty generally applicable, the kindred doctrine of Loose-Fish is still more widely so. It is internationally and universally applicable.

What was America in 1492 but a Loose-Fish, in which Columbus struck the Spanish standard by way of marking it for his royal master and mistress? What was Poland to the Czar? What Greece to the Turk? What India to England? What at last will Mexico be to the United States? All Loose-Fish.

What are the Rights of Man and the Liberties of the World but Loose-Fish? What all men's minds and opinions but Loose-Fish? What is the principle of religious belief in them but a Loose-Fish? What to the pompous pedantic quibblers are the thoughts of thinkers but Loose-Fish? What is the great globe itself but a Loose-Fish? And what are you, reader, but a Loose-Fish and a Fast-Fish, too?
